name: Grandmother Tongue: A Glossary of Lost Languages
creator: Yewande Sobieski-Tanaka
description: Part linguistic archaeology, part elegy, this book documents 200 languages and dialects that have been absorbed beyond recovery into the creole continuum of post-Diaspora Meridian speech, combining rigorous scholarly apparatus with personal essays from the descendants of speakers. Sobieski-Tanaka argues that the Ubiquitous Diaspora, while beautiful, carries a specific grief that must be named and honored rather than celebrated past. The physical edition includes a fold-out map of language-loss patterns across the Great Lakes corridor across 150 years.
medium: physical book (Meridian University Press) and free public neural feed (author's insistence)
cultural_impact: Became an unexpected cross-tier phenomenon — the free neural feed has been accessed by tens of millions, and the physical edition's fold-out map has been reproduced and hung in community spaces from the Gray Zone kitchens to Tier 5 private libraries.
controversy: A vocal minority of critics argue the book is fundamentally conservative, mourning linguistic loss that was also the loss of the structures — including harmful ones — that maintained those languages; Sobieski-Tanaka's response essays have extended the conversation productively.
story_hooks: The fold-out map contains one language listed as 'unverified — source anonymous' that no linguist can identify, and someone is determined to find out if it was real or invented.

A Tier 1 community has begun deliberately reconstructing one of the documented languages as an act of cultural sovereignty, and they want Sobieski-Tanaka involved — but she has complicated feelings about living reconstruction versus honest loss.

A corponation's marketing division has licensed 'Grandmother Tongue' branding for a line of cultural heritage products, and the author's refusal to authorize it is legally complex given the free-access neural feed terms she agreed to.
